release_notes.v0.9.0: feat: `wrapping-up-sessions` now PROVES a squash merge instead of asking about it. A squash merge rewrites a branch into one new commit, so not one of the original commits stays an ancestor of the default branch, and `git branch -d` refuses with "not fully merged" — the same words it uses for a branch that never merged at all. Until now the skill treated that refusal as unresolvable and always stopped to ask. Step 3 now runs a content-equivalence check, `scripts/branch-landed.sh`, and green-lights the delete when the check confirms the changes are already upstream. The script has two arms: `git cherry` compares every branch commit against the upstream patch-ids (this catches a rebase merge or a cherry-pick), and when commits remain it synthesizes a throw-away commit holding the branch's whole tree on top of the merge base and asks `git cherry` whether that single squashed patch is upstream (this catches a squash merge). The verdict is the EXIT CODE — 0 CONTAINED, 1 NOT-CONTAINED, 2 INCONCLUSIVE — and on CONTAINED the one evidence line names the actual squash commit, so the report cites a sha and not only a verdict. Exit 1 and exit 2 both fall through to the existing `git ls-remote` evidence and the confirmation prompt: an absent answer is never read as a negative answer. A `git fetch origin <default-branch>` now runs BEFORE the check, because the only pull in the skill runs AFTER the deletion, and a local default branch that has not yet seen the squash commit would read as never merged. Two properties are documented in the skill body. CONTAINED is one-way proof: patch-id includes the diff context lines, so a default branch that edited the SAME lines before the squash landed reads NOT-CONTAINED for a branch that truly merged — which is why exit 1 asks instead of refusing. And a squash that was later reverted reads CONTAINED, which is the right answer to the question asked and is safe because the step-2 gate already proved every commit is on the remote. `scripts/branch-landed-test.sh` ships the 13-case fixture matrix; every case is checked to be reachable through a real `git branch -d` refusal, and the detector is also proven against a real GitHub squash merge in this repository. The step-2 hard-stop gates are untouched.
release_notes.v0.8.0: feat: `wrapping-up-sessions` now runs in a forked context (`context: fork`) and registers under the bare name `wrapping-up-sessions`. The teardown transcript — the gate checks, the git plumbing, the verification reads — no longer lands in the calling session, which is the session the skill exists to close. Two config changes carry it. The frontmatter `name:` drops the `productivity:` prefix, because the harness already prefixes a plugin skill and the qualified form risks registering the skill under a name no dispatch site resolves (`handoff` in this same plugin already uses the bare form). And `allowed-tools` is now stated: `AskUserQuestion`, `Bash`, `Read` — the whole skill is git plumbing plus the one force-delete confirmation. The skill also stops calling `ExitWorktree`: that tool acts only on the context that calls it, which from a fork is the fork and not the session being closed, so step 3 now names `git worktree remove` as the only removal path instead of a fallback. One behavior follows from this: the CALLING session's folder still points at the removed worktree when the skill finishes, so step 4 reports that fact alongside the safe-to-close signal. Nothing else in the teardown changes — the removal, the branch delete, the checkout, the pull, and the prune all act on the shared checkout and land the same way from a fork. The hard-stop gates, the force-delete confirmation, and the evidence-based verification in step 4 are untouched.
release_notes.v0.7.0: refactor: handoff and dispatch drop their file intermediaries. `handoff` now renders the handoff document directly in the reply instead of saving it to the OS temp directory — the rendered text is the deliverable, and the skill is no longer a byte-verbatim copy of its mattpocock/skills upstream. `dispatch-background-sessions` now forks the current session into the background session (`claude --bg --name <name> --resume "$CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID" --fork-session "<directive>"`) instead of composing a self-contained prompt and writing it to a prompt file: the fork inherits the parent conversation's full context, so the prompt shrinks to a short directive (role reset, work item, disjoint scope, parent pointer, standing constraints, first action) passed via a quoted heredoc. The role reset tells the fork to do the one item and to NOT re-dispatch, fork, or launch further sessions from the dispatch instructions it inherits. If `$CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` is empty the skill stops rather than falling back to `--continue`, which can fork a different conversation. The launch-verify step (`claude logs` after ~15s) and the one-item-per-dispatch rule are kept. Both skill bodies were then reshaped against the August 2026 prompt-engineering principles: `handoff` drops from 4 instructions to 2 and `dispatch-background-sessions` from 12 to 2 (its six-step procedure becomes an outcome plus a 7-line reference block holding the launch snippet), clearing all 7 prompt-lint findings — the emphasis lines, the bare prohibitions that now carry their reason, and the open-ended "any sensitive information" redaction catch-all, which is now a named list. No behaviour changed.
release_notes.v0.6.0: refactor: retire two skills — `wrapping-up-prs` and `designating-session-for-planning`. `wrapping-up-prs` (a ~550-line embedded Workflow carrying Sonar Web API details, per-role model plans, and force-with-lease semantics) duplicated `pr-flow:getting-prs-merged`, `pr-flow:getting-prs-approved`, and `relay:refining-prs`; `designating-session-for-planning` was a thin read-only planning prompt already covered by `superpowers:brainstorming` + `superpowers:writing-plans` and relay's planning skills. Both directories are deleted and every in-repo reference to them is rewritten (to drive a PR to merge-ready, use `relay:refining-prs`). productivity now ships exactly three skills — `handoff`, `dispatch-background-sessions`, and `wrapping-up-sessions` — the set of things nothing else in the ecosystem does.
release_notes.v0.5.0: refactor: wrapping-up-sessions is now exclusively a workspace-teardown skill. Dropped PR resolution and merge-state verification entirely (no more `gh pr view`, no PR-number argument) — the skill assumes the work has already landed and focuses on returning the workspace to a clean default-branch state: exit and remove the worktree, delete the local branch, checkout the default branch, `git pull`, and `git fetch --prune` to drop the stale remote-tracking ref (these stay separate on purpose — a refspec on the command line limits pruning to matching refs, so `git pull --prune <branch>` would not prune the deleted branch). The frontmatter description states that landed-or-abandoned contract explicitly, since removing the merge gate also removed its secondary role as a backstop against a misrouted invocation. The local safety gates are kept and extended, and remain hard stops: clean working tree; nothing unpushed, including a missing upstream; and no in-progress merge/rebase (`git status --porcelain` alone misses this — a conflict resolved in favour of HEAD leaves the tree identical to HEAD while the merge is still open, and removing the worktree would discard the resolution unrecoverably). Because nothing verifies merge state any more, a `git branch -d` refusal is no longer assumed to mean a squash merge — that refusal is identical for a never-merged branch — so the skill gathers remote evidence and asks before force-deleting. Every teardown step is verified with evidence before the session is declared closed, and a failed verification withholds the safe-to-close signal instead of reporting success.
release_notes.v0.4.0: feat: dispatch-background-sessions now records a reference back to the parent session and broadens its trigger. The description matches direct asks like "dispatch a new claude session" / "start a background session to do X" (not only work-item phrasings). At dispatch time the skill captures the parent's `$CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` and embeds it in the composed prompt as a Parent session block, so the dispatched session has a durable pointer home and the user can return with `claude --resume <id>`.
release_notes.v0.3.0: feat: dispatch-background-sessions is now a single call that does the whole dispatch — it writes the composed prompt to a prompt file in the OS temp dir, launches the background session via `claude --bg --name <name> "<prompt>"` so the session starts working immediately (no paste step), verifies via `claude logs` that the session picked up the work, and reports the prompt file as the manual fallback. Adds productivity:wrapping-up-prs — drives an open PR to merge-ready (resolves conflicts, fixes failing CI and Sonar checks, loops until mergeable or awaiting human approval; never merges), completing the command-center loop: designate → dispatch → wrap up PR → wrap up session.
release_notes.v0.2.0: feat: add three portable command-center skills. designating-session-for-planning — read-only command center that scopes work into a prioritized, parallelizable inventory of single-PR-sized items and stops before implementing. dispatch-background-sessions — composes a self-contained, evidence-grounded prompt for one work item, starts an idle background session via `claude --bg`, and prints the prompt to paste in. wrapping-up-sessions — verifies a session's PR is merged and nothing is uncommitted/unpushed, then tears down the local branch + worktree behind hard-stop safety gates. All three are qualified-name (productivity:<slug>) skills, keeping the 0-agent architecture; they are repository-agnostic and carry no project-specific references.
release_notes.v0.1.0: feat: initial release — verbatim handoff skill (from mattpocock/skills) to compact a conversation into a handoff doc for the next agent; skill-only 0-agent plugin.

mission_control_integration.preferred_invocation: invoke the productivity handoff skill to compact the conversation into a handoff document rendered in the reply
